snippet.title: London 1300: The Apocalypse Happened in 1348 (AI Reconstruction)
snippet.description:
In this video! I’m taking you straight back to London in the year 1300, when it was at its medieval peak with 100,000 people.

I’ve used AI to reconstruct what life was actually like there. You’ll see the Old St. Paul’s Cathedral, which was way taller than the one standing today , and the London Bridge, which wasn't just a bridge—it was a floating city with over 140 buildings hanging over the water.

But the most intense part is seeing how this massive city almost hit the end of the world. I explain how they faced three years of nonstop rain that caused a brutal famine , and then the Black Death, which killed about 6 out of every 10 Londoners in just a few months.

It’s crazy to see how the survivors managed to change the social order and rebuild everything from the ruins. Check it out and let me know which era I should reconstruct next!

snippet.title: What New York Looked Like in the 1600s (AI Reconstruction)
snippet.description:
What New York Looked Like in the 1600s (AI Reconstruction)

What was New York like before skyscrapers, stock exchanges, and crowded avenues?
Before it was New York, this place was known as New Amsterdam.

In this video, History Evolution explores New York in the 17th century, when Manhattan was still a small Dutch colonial settlement shaped by trade, geography, and daily survival.

Using original maps, engravings, and written records left behind by those who lived here, we reconstruct these scenes as ultra-realistic visuals, then animate them into motion.
Each reconstruction allows us to move closer than the original artists ever could — to look from above, to stand at street level, and to drift slowly along the water.

Guided by our AI historian Dr. Henry Alden, we follow New Amsterdam as it takes shape:
-Trade between Dutch settlers and the Lenape people
-The settlement viewed from above, still surrounded by nature
-Early Wall Street as a defensive boundary, not a financial center
-The docks of the Dutch West India Company
-Fort Amsterdam seen from the water
-The working canal that became Broad Street
-Markets, taverns, civic spaces, and everyday life
-The peaceful surrender of 1664 under Peter Stuyvesant

This is not a dramatization.
There are no battles, no legends, no modern assumptions.
Only the quiet rhythms of a place still becoming itself.

Through these reconstructed moments, we glimpse the foundations of a future global city — long before it knew what it would become.

snippet.title: What It Was Like Inside Pompeii on Its Final Day (AI Reconstruction)
snippet.description:
On the morning of August 24th, 79 AD, twenty thousand people woke up in Pompeii with absolutely no idea what was coming. They bought bread. They argued at food counters. They trained in gladiatorial barracks. They went about their completely ordinary Tuesday morning — four hours before Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried their entire city forever.

This is not a video about the eruption.

This is a video about the morning before it.

We used AI reconstruction to travel back to Pompeii 79 AD and rebuild the city exactly as it looked on its last day — its streets, its people, its bakeries, its forum, its harbour. Every frame is built from archaeological evidence and historical records. This is Pompeii brought back to life.

What you are about to see will change how you think about ancient Rome, ancient history, and the people who lived it.

🔍 WHAT MAKES THIS VIDEO DIFFERENT

Most Pompeii documentaries focus on the eruption and the destruction. This video focuses on what nobody talks about — the ordinary morning that came before it. The bread still in the ovens. The graffiti still on the walls. The stepping stones still in the street.

The pompeii ruins we see today are not ruins. They are a city frozen mid-sentence.

Using AI history reconstruction we rebuilt that sentence — word by word, street by street, person by person.

Everything in this video is based on:
— Archaeological excavations of Pompeii
— The letters of Pliny the Younger — our primary eyewitness account
— The writings of Pliny the Elder
— The Fiorelli plaster casts — the preserved shapes of pompeii victims
— Documented evidence of pyroclastic surge and volcanic eruption patterns
— Roman daily life records from the Roman Empire period

snippet.title: What It Was Like Living in a House in New York in 1900 | AI Reconstruction
snippet.description:
🗽 New York, 1900: just two years after Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Staten Island were welded into a single city of 3.4 million people, an electrified Fifth Avenue mansion and a windowless Lower East Side tenement bedroom stood barely two streetcar stops apart. AI Reconstruction takes you inside both.

🏛️ Step into the New York household at the precise hinge between the long 19th century and the modern American interior. Discover the dumbbell tenement of the Lower East Side — the railroad flat, the cold-water tap, the cast-iron coal range, the wooden icebox, the shared landing water closet — where Jewish, Italian, Irish and German immigrants stuffed up to twenty families into a single 25-foot lot, and where Jacob Riis had photographed how the other half lived a decade earlier.

🏚️ The documentary then crosses to the brownstone rowhouses of Brooklyn Heights, Park Slope and the Upper West Side, where gas chandeliers, claw-foot tubs and live-in Irish cooks served the Sunday roasts standardised by Fannie Farmer. It visits the limestone Fifth Avenue mansions of the Astors and Vanderbilts, the pushcart markets of Hester Street, the German bakeries of Kleindeutschland and the oyster cellars of Canal Street, and closes on the eve of the New Tenement House Act of April 1901.

🔔 If you enjoy this kind of careful reconstruction of vanished interiors, subscribe to History Reconstruction, hit 👍 and turn on notifications so the next vanished world arrives in your feed.

snippet.title: ⚔️ AD 77-84 | Rome in Scotland | Part I
snippet.description:
What you're seeing:
The Agricola campaign across Britain and into Scotland, from a demoralized province to the first clash with the Caledonians. Every scene is reconstructed from Tacitus' biography of his father-in-law, Gnaeus Julius Agricola, the Roman governor who nearly conquered all of Britain.

Where is this?
Southern Britain, Wales, Anglesey, the Scottish Lowlands, the Clyde-Forth isthmus, the western coast opposite Ireland, and the east coast of Scotland. Locations are based on Frere's campaign map in "Britannia" and cross-referenced against Tacitus' descriptions.

Who are these people?
Agricola was a Roman senator and military commander who served as governor of Britain from AD 77 to 84. He had first served in Britain as a young officer during Boudica's revolt in AD 60. The Caledonians were the tribal peoples of northern Scotland who had never been conquered by Rome.

Why does this matter?
This is the lead-up to the Battle of Mons Graupius (AD 84), the largest battle ever fought in Scotland and one of the few ancient battles described in detail by a contemporary source. Part II covers the battle itself, including the famous speeches of Calgacus and Agricola.

Outcome and how we know: Tacitus,
"The Agricola" (c. AD 98). Tacitus was Agricola's son-in-law and wrote this biography shortly after Agricola's death. It is the only surviving firsthand account of Roman campaigns in Scotland. All dialogue in this video is reconstructed.

Latin, Ancient British and Ancient Caledonian dialogue are reconstructed. No written Caledonian texts survive.

snippet.title: How Pirates Survived Freezing Nights at Sea Without Heating in 1715
snippet.description:
What was life on a pirate ship really like in 1715? Forty-seven pirates aboard a wooden vessel in the freezing North Atlantic faced a problem nobody talks about in the legends of the Golden Age of Piracy — they could not light a fire. Not a brazier, not a stove, not even a candle past sundown. A single spark in the orlop deck could burn the entire ship to the waterline, and on the open ocean there was no rescue, no land, no second chance. So how did real pirates survive freezing nights at sea without any heating?
In this AI historical reconstruction, we rebuild a single night below decks on a Golden Age pirate ship — the cramped hammocks, the single guttering oil lamp, the layered wool clothing, the forgotten body-heat rituals, and the brutal shipboard rules that kept the wooden hull from becoming a coffin. This is the maritime history of real pirate life — not the rum, not the parrots, not the Captain Jack fantasy. This is what survival actually looked like on a wooden ship in the Age of Sail when the temperature dropped and the wind tore through the rigging for nights on end.
If you enjoy historical reconstructions that show you how people actually lived in the past, subscribe to Worlds Before Us for more cinematic deep-dives into the forgotten realities of history.

🎬 HOW WE BUILT THIS VIDEO — AI HISTORICAL RECONSTRUCTION
At Worlds Before Us, we use a combination of academic historical research and modern AI image and video generation tools to visually reconstruct lives that no camera was ever there to capture. Every frame in this video was generated from period-accurate references — 18th-century shipwright records, surviving sailor clothing, contemporary paintings of ship interiors, and primary-source descriptions of below-deck conditions — and then composed into cinematic sequences. The result lets you see, not just hear, what survival actually looked like on a freezing pirate ship in 1715. We do not invent — we reconstruct, frame by frame, from the historical record.

📚 HISTORICAL SOURCES USED FOR THIS SCRIPT
The script for this video draws on the following published works and primary sources for its claims about Golden Age pirate life, shipboard conditions, fire restrictions, and cold-weather survival:
• David Cordingly — Under the Black Flag: The Romance and the Reality of Life Among the Pirates (Random House, 1995). The standard work on separating pirate myth from documented reality.
• Marcus Rediker — Villains of All Nations: Atlantic Pirates in the Golden Age (Beacon Press, 2004). Academic history of the 1716–1726 Golden Age pirates, including crew sizes, articles, and conditions.
• Marcus Rediker — Between the Devil and the Deep Blue Sea: Merchant Seamen, Pirates, and the Anglo-American Maritime World, 1700–1750 (Cambridge University Press, 1987). Definitive source on daily life aboard early-18th-century Atlantic ships, including sleeping arrangements, watch rotations, and cold-weather practices.
• Colin Woodard — The Republic of Pirates: Being the True and Surprising Story of the Caribbean Pirates and the Man Who Brought Them Down (Harcourt, 2007). Narrative history of the Nassau-based pirate republic.
• Peter Earle — Sailors: English Merchant Seamen 1650–1775 (Methuen, 1998) and The Pirate Wars (Methuen, 2003). Source for shipboard fire regulations, galley use, and the structural reasons no open flame was permitted below decks at night.
• Captain Charles Johnson — A General History of the Robberies and Murders of the Most Notorious Pyrates (T. Warner, 1724). Contemporaneous account written within a decade of the events depicted.
• William Dampier — A New Voyage Round the World (1697). First-hand period account of conditions aboard late-17th and early-18th century ships in cold Atlantic latitudes.
• Royal Museums Greenwich and the National Maritime Museum, London — collections and digitized archives of period sailor clothing, hammock construction, ship-board lighting fixtures, and surviving 18th-century shipwright plans.
